Keys can be released with policy from a managed HSM such as Azure Managed HSM or Azure Key Vault into the Azure Integrated HSM, which is FIPS 140-3 Level 3 certified just like the HSMs behind those services, keeping the key inside that boundary from HSM to server where the hardware is mapped into the VM for operations. A demo signing payloads with an AKV key showed the benefit, comparing signing throughput when using Azure Key Vault directly (about 640 operations/second) versus releasing the key locally (about 18,800 operations/second) with no loss of security.

This enables custom, non-boxing implementations or retrofitting existing hand-rolled union classes.

entities.canonicalName: Azure Container Storage distributed cache (early access)
entities.tagline: An AKS-native distributed cache where every GPU node acts as both cache and client over local NVMe RAID, delivering roughly 2.5x faster model loading and hitting Blob only once when many pods start together.
entities.longDescription: To solve the cold-start problem where many pods each pull a large model from Blob at once (e.g., 100 pods pulling a 70B/140GB model equals 14TB causing throttling and NIC saturation), Microsoft built a distributed cache inside the AKS cluster itself with zero changes to the workflow on top—Hugging Face Loader, BlobFuse, and the Run AI Streamer all sit on it unchanged. Every GPU node acts as both cache and client, with local NVMe RAID holding hot data served at NVMe speed via zero-copy sendfile, and missing data coming over the network from a peer. The first pod warms the cache and the next 99 read from inside the cluster, delivering roughly 2.5x faster model loading on AKS while Blob is hit exactly once. It is in early access now; users can scan a QR code to sign up.

entities.tagline: Each named replica gets its own connection string, buffer pool, and RBPEX (Resilient Buffer Pool Extension) L2 cache, isolating read workloads from primary writes over the same up-to-128 TB dataset.
entities.longDescription: A major advantage of Azure SQL Hyperscale is named replicas, where each readable copy gets its own connection string. Each named replica has its own buffer pool (memory) and L2 cache—called RBPEX, the Resilient Buffer Pool Extension—giving it its own working set that is distinct from any other named replica, while all share the same underlying dataset of up to 128 TB. This isolation lets writes on the primary remain unaffected by reads, so customers can run continuous writes on the primary while pointing agents at a named replica for vector distance and cosine similarity work.

entities.canonicalName: LLM-native alert grouping delivers the largest savings
entities.tagline: Since most alerts during an outage are duplicates of one root cause, letting the LLM generate and persist grouping rules avoids linear per-alert cost while avoiding the pitfalls of deterministic rules.
entities.longDescription: Yellin identifies the biggest optimization as the fact that most alerts are duplicates; in a big production outage, the 500 incoming alerts are mostly duplicates of the same cause, so investigating each one naively incurs a linear cost. Grouping dramatically reduces this, but it must be LLM-native rather than using old-school deterministic rules, which either group too aggressively (merging different root causes) or not aggressively enough (missing alerts with different names from different systems). Their approach lets the LLM generate the grouping rules, persist them for a period, and control the policy on what triggers reinvestigations.

entities.longDescription: Memory safety is a massive two-release project spanning .NET 11 and 12, in preview in .NET 11. In this release the team is defining a set of language changes, applying them to System.Private.CoreLib (the bottom-most managed library), and making changes so they and others need to use Unsafe less, including in SIMD code. The key takeaway, detailed in a blog post written about a week prior, is that the Unsafe keyword is being redesigned to mean a reviewable caller contract rather than establishing an unsafe context, with APIs like Unsafe and MemoryMarshal marked with this contract; .NET 12 finishes the work.

entities.tagline: A cross-platform, declarative library that dynamically composes a right-sized container per agent action by matching developer, user, and IT policy against available OS primitives.
entities.longDescription: The Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) Library is introduced to create containers based on policy, providing an isolation boundary proportionate to the risk and action an agent performs. Developers and agents declare the security requirements of the agent and its individual actions, and the library compiles those and matches them against system policies and policies defined by IT through familiar deployment, management, and monitoring tools. Once a match occurs, the MXC library examines the native OS platform primitives and assembles the right container for the job, a process called dynamic composition. This enables least-privilege enforcement where each action runs in its own sandbox with policy defining just what it can do.

entities.tagline: A new Ethernet-based networking protocol co-developed with OpenAI that packet-sprays across independent "planes" to survive congestion and link failures during massive training jobs
entities.longDescription: MRC (Multi-Path Reliable Connection) is a new Ethernet-based networking protocol developed with OpenAI and a growing consortium of partners, replacing RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) in the Fairwater data centers that switched from InfiniBand to Ethernet. It is designed to be resilient during massive synchronous training jobs connecting up to 100,000 GPUs, where congestion or a single failure could otherwise force a costly restart from a checkpoint. MRC sprays packets across independent network domains called planes, so when a link is dropped the spraying rebalances across the remaining available planes. A demo showed two servers sending 4 GB payloads over 4 switches, achieving roughly 95 GB/s by spraying across 8 planes at about 12 GB per plane.

entities.canonicalName: Native JSON type and path-specific JSON indexes
entities.tagline: SQL stores JSON as a pre-parsed binary (ANSI JSON type, no longer NVARCHAR(MAX)), cutting JSON storage by 30–50% and allowing indexing of a specific JSON path rather than the whole document.
entities.longDescription: Microsoft SQL recently introduced a native JSON type and JSON indexes, replacing the earlier NVARCHAR(MAX) approach. The native JSON type is ANSI-compliant and stored as a pre-parsed binary, which makes JSON storage 30 to 50% smaller. Unlike other relational databases that index the entire JSON document, Microsoft SQL lets you index a particular path of the JSON (e.g. only the device attribute), and the JSON index will pick that path. JSON also retains schema flexibility for documents with varying attributes.

entities.canonicalName: Unions enforce exhaustiveness in switch expressions
entities.tagline: once a value is typed as a union, the compiler warns when not all case types (including null where applicable) are handled.
entities.longDescription: Once a value is typed as a union (e.g. a union of pets), the compiler can prove whether a switch expression is exhaustive, removing the earlier warning once all case types are covered. Commenting out one of the case types brings the warning back, demonstrating that the compiler ensures all cases—and nothing but the cases—are handled. The system is smart enough that if the union includes a nullable case (e.g. a nullable bird), null must also be handled for the switch to be exhaustive.

entities.longDescription: The WinApp CLI, announced earlier this year, is a command-line tool installable via WinGet ('winget install winapp') that lets developers and agents package applications and run them with package identity without Visual Studio. It works with existing frameworks—for example running a Rust console application—so developers can keep their current framework and extend it with Windows APIs.

entities.canonicalName: WinUI drops its version number, signaling long-term commitment
entities.tagline: WinUI 3 will now be referred to simply as "WinUI" to convey there is no intention of building yet another new framework or a massive breaking change.
entities.longDescription: In response to community questions about whether Microsoft is serious about sticking with the framework, the team announced that WinUI 3 (now four years old) will be referred to simply as "WinUI," dropping the version number to signal there is no intention of building yet another new framework or making a massive breaking change. The team is pushing to stretch WinUI to be accessible for any use case and is integrating it into the shell at a faster rate, with many first-party Microsoft features being built on top of WinUI. They emphasized commitment to moving WinUI forward and hope to see broader third-party and enterprise adoption.

entities.tagline: A built-in way to create, run, and interact with Linux containers natively on Windows, shipping with the standard WSL update and exposed as an API for use inside native applications, plus enterprise management controls
entities.longDescription: WSL containers is a built-in way to create, run, and interact with Linux containers directly on Windows, so containers just work natively out-of-the-box for local development, AI/ML workflows, and containerized testing. It ships with the standard WSL update with no extra configuration, and includes WSLC, a binary for creating, running, and interacting with containers without third-party tools. Usage is as simple as listing containers (e.g., 'WSLC container LS'), attaching to a running container's Linux shell, and detaching when done.

entities.tagline: Opt-in feature compiling XAML to readable, debuggable C# with cited gains of ~1,000% faster inflation, 99% less debug memory, and reduced app memory; default in .NET 11
entities.longDescription: XAML source generation is an opt-in feature that uses Roslyn to generate readable, debuggable C# source from XAML, rather than the current XAML-C compilation to intermediate language. It delivers faster debug and release performance by flipping one bit, with cited gains of 1,000% faster inflation, 99% less debug memory, faster release, and less app memory, with the biggest improvement in debug builds. It also eliminates differences between debug and release builds (such as trimmed APIs breaking at runtime). It is opt-in in .NET 10 and will become the default in .NET 11.
